results.reply:
Exactly right — and notice what that rules out: the model isn't spell-checking, it isn't searching, it's doing math on a list of numbers from the very first step.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Once your prompt is a sequence of numbers, the model needs to figure out what those numbers *mean in relation to each other* — and that's where the **attention mechanism** comes in.

Attention lets every token "look at" every other token in your prompt and decide how much to care about it.

[KEY]Attention is how the model tracks relationships between words — which words modify which, what a pronoun refers to, how context shifts meaning.[/KEY]

[EX]Take the sentence "I went to the bank." Does "bank" mean a riverbank or a financial institution? A tokenizer can't tell — but the attention mechanism weighs the surrounding tokens ("went to the") and picks up on contextual clues. If the sentence were "I went to the bank to deposit my check," attention would heavily weight "deposit" and "check" when processing "bank."[/EX]

This happens across dozens of layers, with the model constantly updating its sense of what each token means given all the others around it.

[Q]
What is the attention mechanism's main job?
A) Memorizing facts from training data
B) Translating tokens back into readable words
C) Tracking how tokens relate to and influence each other
ANS: C
[/Q]

Exactly right — the words are gone by the time the model starts "thinking." What travels forward is purely numerical.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers don't just sit in a list — they get transformed into something richer called an **embedding**, and then the model runs a process called **attention** to figure out how every token relates to every other token in your prompt.

Think about this sentence: *"I went to the bank."*

Does "bank" mean a riverbank or a financial institution? A human uses context — the surrounding words — to know instantly.

[KEY]The attention mechanism is how the model does the same thing: it weighs how much each token should "pay attention to" every other token, so meaning comes from relationships, not just individual words.[/KEY]

[EX]In "She poured the water from the pitcher because it was empty," the model's attention heads figure out that "it" refers to "pitcher" — not "water" — by measuring which earlier tokens are most relevant to resolving that pronoun. This happens across all tokens simultaneously, in parallel.[/EX]

After attention has built up a rich picture of what everything means in context, the model does one final thing: it predicts the single most likely *next* token — then repeats the whole process to predict the one after that, and so on, until your response is complete.

[Q]
Why does the attention mechanism exist?
A) To speed up the model by skipping unimportant words
B) To look up facts in a built-in knowledge database
C) To capture how the meaning of each token depends on the tokens around it
ANS: C
[/Q]

Exactly right — and notice what that rules out: there's no dictionary lookup, no database, no spell-checker. Just a list of numbers flowing into the next stage.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers don't stay as flat integers — they get transformed into something richer called an **embedding**.

Think of an embedding as a location in a giant invisible map — a space with hundreds of dimensions — where words that *mean similar things* end up *near each other*.

[KEY]An embedding turns each token into a point in high-dimensional space, so the model can reason about meaning, not just identity.[/KEY]

[EX]In a well-trained embedding space, the token "king" sits close to "queen" and "monarch" — and far from "bicycle." The famous example: "king" − "man" + "woman" ≈ "queen." The geometry encodes real-world relationships.[/EX]

Here's why this matters for your prompt: the sentence "I went to the bank" is genuinely ambiguous — river bank or financial bank? The embedding for "bank" shifts depending on the surrounding tokens. The model uses an **attention mechanism** to weigh which nearby words matter most when interpreting each token.

That's what lets it pick the right meaning from context.

[Q]
What is the main job of the attention mechanism?
A) Storing facts the model memorized during training
B) Deciding which other tokens in the sequence matter most for understanding each token
C) Converting the model's output back into readable words
ANS: B
[/Q]

Exactly right — the model never touches raw text again after that first conversion step.

Now here's where it gets interesting. Those numbers don't just sit in a list — they get transformed into something richer called an **embedding**: a point in a vast mathematical space where *meaning* shapes the geography.

Words with similar meanings end up near each other in that space. "King" and "queen" are close. "Bank" (river) and "bank" (finance) start in the same spot — but the model uses an **attention mechanism** to look at surrounding words and figure out which neighborhood they actually belong in.

[KEY]Attention lets the model weigh every other token in your prompt when deciding what each token means — so context shapes interpretation, not just the word itself.[/KEY]

[EX]The sentence "I went to the bank to fish" and "I went to the bank to deposit cash" use the identical word "bank" — but attention pulls it toward completely different meanings based on "fish" vs. "deposit."[/EX]

After attention does its work, the model has a rich, context-aware representation of your entire prompt.

Then comes the final move: it predicts the single most probable *next token* — and repeats that, one token at a time, until the response is done.

[Q]
What is the model actually doing when it generates a response, word by word?
A) Retrieving a stored answer from a database
B) Translating your words into another language internally
C) Repeatedly predicting the single most likely next token
ANS: C
[/Q]

Exactly right — and that detail matters more than it sounds, because everything the model does from here operates purely on those numbers, never on "meaning" the way a human feels it.

Now, those numbers don't just sit in a list. The model needs to know that "bank" in "river bank" means something totally different from "bank" in "bank account." That's where the next step comes in: **embedding space**.

Each token-number gets translated into a point in a vast mathematical space — hundreds or thousands of dimensions. Words with related meanings end up *geometrically close* to each other in that space. "Doctor" and "physician" are nearby.

"Doctor" and "skateboard" are far apart.

[KEY]Embeddings turn token numbers into coordinates in meaning-space, so the model can do math on relationships between words.[/KEY]

[EX]The famous demo: in embedding space, the vector "king" minus "man" plus "woman" lands almost exactly on "queen." The model learned that relationship purely from seeing patterns in text — no one programmed it in.[/EX]

Then the model's **attention mechanism** looks at all the tokens in your prompt simultaneously and asks: *which other tokens should each token pay attention to?* That's how it figures out which "bank" you meant — by noticing the surrounding context.

[Q]
Why do LLMs use embeddings instead of just passing the raw token numbers into the model?
A) Raw numbers are too large to store efficiently
B) Embeddings encode relationships between words as geometry the model can compute on
C) Embeddings translate text back into plain English for processing
ANS: B
[/Q]
